opening: For an hour, the square belongs to a game. People accept an invented constraint, argue about a rule, attempt something difficult, and laugh at a failure that would be frightening elsewhere. Play creates a temporary world in which effort need not be justified by survival.

title: Hospitality Across Difference
summary: Welcome encounter while respecting boundaries and reciprocal responsibilities.
statement: Therefore, establish ordinary practices that help strangers and newcomers participate with dignity. Make expectations understandable, offer meaningful choices, and allow mutual learning within fair boundaries.
first_move: Ask someone unfamiliar with a community space to describe their first ten minutes there. Identify the point at which they felt unsure, unwelcome, or dependent on insider knowledge. Change that condition and test the welcome again with a different newcomer.
opening: The visitor does not know where to sit, what food contains, which customs matter, or how to decline politely. The host may not know what the visitor needs. Hospitality begins by making this uncertainty easier to navigate.

title: Freedom to Be Strange
summary: Leave room for eccentricity, experimentation, and harmless refusal.
statement: Therefore, protect harmless eccentricity, unconventional relationships, minority expression, and experiments in living. Require a concrete account of harm before using collective power to enforce conformity.
first_move: Review one rule that limits expression or participation. State the concrete harm it prevents and examine whether a less restrictive rule would address that harm. Remove requirements whose main function is to make everyone resemble the people already in charge.
opening: The unusual person is tolerated until a committee asks whether their life is useful, respectable, or representative. A society can speak warmly about diversity while making everyday existence difficult for anyone who departs too far from its preferred forms.

title: Grief With Somewhere to Go
summary: Give private and collective loss companionship, expression, and time.
statement: Therefore, make room for mourning in private and collective life. Offer practical support, voluntary forms of remembrance, and continuing companionship without prescribing a timetable or a single acceptable expression.
first_move: Choose one setting where loss is currently handled through silence or a brief formal gesture. Ask affected people what ongoing support would be welcome. Establish one dependable practice that remains available after attention has moved elsewhere.
opening: After the first week, the messages become less frequent. The person who has lost someone or something remains inside a changed world while ordinary schedules resume around them.

title: Beauty Without Possession
summary: Expand opportunities to enjoy what need not be individually owned.
statement: Therefore, create opportunities to encounter beauty through shared access, care, attention, and temporary participation. Protect the places, beings, and makers involved from being reduced to objects of possession.
first_move: Identify one source of beauty people could enjoy more fairly without owning it. Work with its makers or caretakers to improve access while funding care and respecting limits. Notice whether the arrangement deepens attention or simply increases consumption.
opening: The view is beautiful until a fence makes it available only to those who can pay. The object is beautiful until its removal leaves the place it came from diminished. Admiration can become a desire to control what should remain encountered on other terms.

title: Begin With a Place
summary: Choose a real place, its inhabitants, and a tractable need.
statement: Therefore, begin where you can observe consequences, form relationships, and accept responsibility. Learn the place before deciding which patterns it needs, and connect local action to wider obligations.
first_move: Spend time in one place without proposing a solution. Ask three people with different relationships to it what works, what hurts, and what they fear losing. Write a short account they can correct, then choose one question worth investigating together.
opening: The book is large enough to make action feel small. A reader can spend years comparing civilizations while the leaking roof, inaccessible doorway, neglected stream, or lonely neighbor remains unchanged.

title: Map Who Bears the Cost
summary: Trace benefits, burdens, dependencies, and missing voices.
statement: Therefore, identify who benefits, who bears costs, who decides, and who cannot speak within the process. Follow consequences across places, species, institutions, and time before fixing the design.
first_move: For one live proposal, draw four columns: benefits, burdens, decision power, and missing voices. Put names or clearly defined groups into each. Find the largest mismatch between burden and influence, then change the process to address it.
opening: The proposal describes benefits for users and savings for the organization. Missing are the night worker, the downstream community, the animal habitat, and the person who will inherit the maintenance obligation.

title: Assemble a Working Language
summary: Connect the patterns needed for one coherent intervention.
statement: Therefore, select a small group of connected patterns around a concrete purpose. Make their tensions explicit and develop a design that serves them together rather than treating them as independent boxes to check.
first_move: Choose five patterns for a current project. Write one sentence explaining what each requires in this place, then identify the hardest conflict among them. Produce two plausible designs that handle the conflict differently and compare their consequences with affected people.
opening: One pattern rarely resolves a real problem. A public space needs maintenance, access, beauty, safety, freedom, and rules for sharing it. Applying one principle without its neighbors can produce the very harm the broader language tries to prevent.

title: Small Trials With Real Boundaries
summary: Test safely with consent and limits on exposure.
statement: Therefore, test uncertain proposals through bounded trials with clear purposes, informed participation where relevant, stop conditions, and a credible ending. Protect people from bearing serious risks merely because a project is labeled experimental.
first_move: Write a one-page trial agreement naming the learning question, boundaries, responsibilities, stop conditions, and ending plan. Ask an affected person to identify the promise they would rely on most. Make that promise credible before beginning.
opening: A pilot project is called temporary, but people reorganize their lives around it. Data are collected that cannot be recalled. A commercial relationship becomes difficult to leave. Small scale does not automatically make an experiment harmless or reversible.

title: Independent Eyes
summary: Invite reviewers who can challenge incentives and conclusions.
statement: Therefore, invite qualified scrutiny from people who can examine consequential claims without depending on the project's success. Give them access, a clear remit, and a route for findings to affect decisions.
first_move: Identify the claim your project most needs an outsider to believe. Invite a qualified reviewer to test it, provide the evidence they reasonably need, and agree in advance how an unfavorable finding would change the next decision.
opening: People close to a project see details outsiders miss. They also have reasons to defend it: effort already invested, relationships at stake, and a hope that the work matters. Independent scrutiny can reveal what commitment makes difficult to notice.

title: Publish the Failures
summary: Share negative results while protecting personal privacy.
statement: Therefore, share useful accounts of failure, limitation, and correction alongside success. Preserve enough context for others to judge what the experience means, while protecting people from unnecessary exposure or blame.
first_move: Write a short account of one attempt that did not work as hoped. Include what you expected, what happened, what you still do not know, and what another practitioner should consider before trying it. Invite someone affected to correct the account before sharing it.
opening: The successful project becomes a case study. The failed version disappears into a drawer. The next community repeats the same mistakes because the public record contains ambition and celebration but little account of what proved difficult.

title: Make Better Practices Easier
summary: Remove obstacles in defaults, financing, training, and rules.
statement: Therefore, redesign ordinary conditions so that beneficial practices are accessible, affordable, intelligible, and convenient. Preserve meaningful choice while removing unnecessary friction from doing the right thing.
first_move: Follow a willing participant through one beneficial practice from intention to completion. Record every point where they need unusual effort, money, knowledge, or permission. Remove the most consequential unnecessary obstacle and check whether the practice becomes easier for people with fewer resources.
opening: The responsible choice requires a form, a special request, a higher price, and a long journey. The harmful choice is available by default. Repeated appeals to virtue will struggle against an environment organized in the opposite direction.

title: Return and Reconsider
summary: Revisit consequences, repair harms, and revise or retire.
statement: Therefore, attach review to consequential commitments from the beginning. Revisit purposes, outcomes, burdens, and assumptions at intervals suited to the stakes, and act on what has changed.
first_move: Choose one significant commitment without a review date. Set a proportionate date, identify who should participate, and state which evidence would justify changing or ending the arrangement. Allocate the time and authority needed for the review to have consequences.
opening: The opening ceremony ends, the report is filed, and attention moves elsewhere. Years later, the arrangement still carries the authority of a decision made under conditions that no longer exist.

title: Keep the Language Open
summary: Preserve attribution, competing versions, and freedom to improve.
statement: Therefore, treat these patterns as a revisable common instrument. Preserve their history, invite evidence and dissent, and keep the process of changing them accessible to people who bear their consequences.
first_move: Choose the pattern you most doubt. Find a situation that tests it, record what happens, and propose a correction that another person can examine. Begin there. Somewhere, a thousand years from now, someone may inherit the room you left them to disagree.
opening: The final pattern cannot be a lock. If this book succeeds, people will discover circumstances it misunderstands, beings it neglects, and possibilities its authors could not imagine. Some patterns will need new forms. Others may deserve replacement.
